mainTopic: רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון on courtyards, a חורבה between two courtyards, and the משנה of a large area opening into a small one
overview: The גמרא first challenges רבי יוחנן's ruling that the הלכה follows רבי שמעון, who treats courtyards as one domain. The challenge comes from a סתם משנה that forbids bringing fruit 'down' from a wall between two courtyards. The גמרא answers that 'down' means into the houses. It then dismisses רבי חייא's stricter ברייתא, since רבי did not teach that in the משנה. Next, רב הונא and חייא בר רב argue about a חורבה between two courtyards when only one courtyard made an עירוב. The key point in that argument is that utensils are kept in a courtyard but not in a ruin. A new משנה follows: when a large roof or courtyard opens into a small one, the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden. רב and שמואל each explain why the משנה teaches both cases. Finally, the sages learn from the משנה that residents of the large courtyard count in the small one but not the reverse. They begin illustrating this with vines and כלאים, and that illustration continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Challenging רבי יוחנן from the משנה about fruit on a wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יוחנן can rule like רבי שמעון when he also said the הלכה follows a סתם משנה. A סתם משנה about a wall between two courtyards seems to treat the courtyards as separate domains.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יוחנן really say this? But רבי יוחנן said the הלכה follows an unattributed משנה. And we learned: a wall between two courtyards that is ten טפחים high and four wide gets two separate עירובין, not one. If there was fruit on top of it, people from each side may climb up and eat it there, as long as they do not bring it down. So why can't they bring it down, if all courtyards are one domain?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי יוחנן's ruling, made on the previous amud, that the הלכה follows רבי שמעון. It uses a סתם משנה that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן has a rule: the הלכה always follows a סתם משנה. The משנה forbids bringing the fruit 'down', which sounds like down into the courtyards. That would mean each courtyard is its own domain, which contradicts רבי שמעון's view that all courtyards are one domain.

keyTerms.meaning: An unattributed משנה, stated with no named author; usually the accepted הלכה
They make an עירוב (join areas together so carrying is allowed)
Provided that / only on condition that

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse two different questions. רבי שמעון's leniency does not ask whether you may carry from a house into a courtyard. It asks whether objects that were already in one courtyard may be moved into another courtyard. The whole debate here is about where 'down' leads.
steps.whyThisMatters: It pits two of רבי יוחנן's own rules against each other: following רבי שמעון, and following a סתם משנה.

phrases.english: Did Rabbi Yochanan really say this?
phrases.notes: Refers to his ruling that the הלכה follows רבי שמעון

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
The law follows an unattributed Mishnah.
And we learned: a wall between two courtyards,
ten handbreadths high and four wide —
they make two eiruvin, but they do not make one eiruv.
If there was fruit on top of it —
these people climb up from here and eat,
and those people climb up from there and eat,
provided they do not bring it down below?
phrases.notes: He's really asking: why not, if the courtyards count as one domain?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָכִי? וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's ruling earlier (that the הלכה follows רבי שמעון)
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that the הלכה follows רבי שמעון (courtyards are one domain)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Contradiction between two of רבי יוחנן's statements. A סתם משנה, which he follows, forbids bringing the fruit 'down', implying the courtyards are separate domains.

steps.title: Down means down into the houses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that 'down' in the משנה means down into the houses, not into the courtyards.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'down' mean? Down into the houses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן by reinterpreting one word in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה only forbids bringing the fruit into the houses, it says nothing against moving it into the courtyards. So the משנה can fit רבי שמעון's view after all, and רבי יוחנן's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: What is / what does it mean

phrases.english: What does "down" mean —
down into the houses.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Down' meant down into the courtyards, making the courtyards separate domains
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Down' means down into the houses; the courtyards may still count as one domain

steps.title: רבי חייא's ברייתא forbids even eating in one's own courtyard
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא taught by רבי חייא says each person may not even stand in his own courtyard and eat the fruit. That clearly forbids the courtyards, not only the houses.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי חייא taught: only on condition that this one does not stand in his place and eat, and that one does not stand in his place and eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 2, using a ברייתא of רבי חייא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'His place' means down in his own courtyard. If even eating the fruit while standing there is forbidden, then 'down' must include the courtyards, and the original challenge returns.

keyTerms.meaning: A student of רבי who compiled ברייתות

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Chiya teach:

phrases.aramaic: וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא זֶה עוֹמֵד בִּמְקוֹמוֹ וְאוֹכֵל,
phrases.english: provided that this one does not stand in his place and eat,
and that one does not stand in his place and eat!

steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'down' means only into the houses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חייא's ברייתא explicitly forbids eating the fruit in one's own courtyard, so the courtyards are included in the restriction

steps.title: רבי חייא cannot add what רבי did not teach
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers רבינא: since רבי did not teach this restriction in the משנה, רבי חייא's version does not decide the meaning of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: if רבי did not teach it, where would רבי חייא get it from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the ברייתא as a reason to reread the משנה. The משנה follows its own simple reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי compiled the משנה, and רבי חייא was his student. Whatever רבי left out cannot be forced into the משנה based on a student's ברייתא. So the סתם משנה stays consistent with רבי שמעון, and רבי יוחנן's two rules no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יהודה הנשיא, the compiler of the משנה
From where does he know it?

steps.whatToRemember: The challenge to רבי יוחנן is resolved. 'Down' in the משנה means into the houses. רבי חייא's ברייתא cannot override how the משנה itself reads, because רבי did not teach that restriction.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets a principle: the משנה's own wording is not reshaped to match a ברייתא when רבי himself did not teach that detail.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי speaking to רבינא.

phrases.english: If Rebbe did not teach it,
from where would Rabbi Chiya know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי רַבִּי לֹא שְׁנָאָהּ, רַבִּי חִיָּיא מִנַּיִן לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 3 by dismissing the ברייתא's authority over the משנה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the authority of the conflicting source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי חייא's ברייתא shows how to read the משנה
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is read on its own terms, since רבי did not teach the restriction, so רבי יוחנן's position stands

steps.title: רב הונא on a ruin between two courtyards
steps.stepSummary: Two courtyards have a חורבה between them, and only one courtyard made an עירוב. רב הונא rules that the courtyard without an עירוב may use the ruin, but the one with an עירוב may not, in case they carry house utensils into the ruin.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: two courtyards with one ruin between them. One courtyard made an עירוב and the other did not. רב הונא said: we give the ruin to the one that did not make an עירוב, but not to the one that did. Otherwise they might come to take house utensils out into the ruin.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic opens. The גמרא brings an אמוראic ruling about who gets to use a ruin that sits between two courtyards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard that made an עירוב may carry from its houses into its courtyard. People there might then carry house utensils straight into the ruin, which is forbidden because the ruin was not included in any עירוב. The courtyard with no עירוב already may not carry from its houses at all, so that concern does not apply, and it may use the ruin.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces an אמוראic dispute)
A ruin; an abandoned, broken-down space (here, one that opens into both courtyards)
We give / grant the use of

steps.confusionAlert: It seems backwards that the courtyard that made an עירוב is restricted. The reason is that their permission to carry from the houses creates the risk. The courtyard without an עירוב has no such permission, so there is no risk.

phrases.english: It was stated:
two courtyards with one ruin between them,
one made an eiruv and one did not make an eiruv,
Rav Huna said:
we give it to the one that did not make an eiruv,
but to the one that made an eiruv — no.

phrases.aramaic: דִילְמָא אָתֵי לְאַפּוֹקֵי מָאנֵי דְבָתִּים לְחוּרְבָּה.
phrases.english: Lest they come to take house utensils out to the ruin.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר: שְׁתֵּי חֲצֵירוֹת וְחוּרְבָּה אַחַת בֵּינֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic, separate from the previous challenge
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ruin is given to the courtyard without an עירוב, not to the one with an עירוב, because of a decree that people might carry house utensils into the ruin

steps.title: חייא בר רב: the ruin belongs to both courtyards, so both are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: חייא בר רב disagrees with רב הונא. He holds that the courtyard with an עירוב also has rights in the חורבה, so the two courtyards restrict each other and neither may use it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And חייא בר רב said: the ruin belongs even to the courtyard that made an עירוב, and so both courtyards are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא, חייא בר רב, argues on רב הונא's ruling about the ruin between the two courtyards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא said only the courtyard without an עירוב may use the ruin. חייא בר רב says the courtyard with an עירוב also has a share in it. Since two separate groups now share the ruin without joining together, each forbids the other, and nobody may carry there.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, the son of רב, who disagrees with רב הונא here
Even to the one (courtyard) that made an עירוב

phrases.english: And Chiyya bar Rav said:
[The ruin is given] even to the one that made an eruv,
phrases.notes: So both courtyards have rights in the ruin.

phrases.english: and [so] both are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Argues with רב הונא's ruling in step 5
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both courtyards have rights in the חורבה, so they forbid each other and neither may use it.

steps.title: Proof: a courtyard without an עירוב is never given to one with an עירוב
steps.stepSummary: חייא בר רב (or the גמרא for him) proves his view. If both could use the ruin, why do the Sages never let a courtyard with an עירוב use a neighboring courtyard that has no עירוב?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say both courtyards are permitted, then why do we not give a courtyard that did not make an עירוב to a courtyard that did make one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof for חייא בר רב's strict view by comparing the ruin to an ordinary neighboring courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule that a courtyard with an עירוב may not use a courtyard without one. If no worry existed, that should be allowed. So, the argument goes, the same worry should forbid the ruin too.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (introduces a possible opposing view)
We do not give / assign (usage rights)
A courtyard that did not make an עירוב

phrases.english: And if you say both are permitted,
for what reason do we not give
a courtyard that did not make an eruv to a courtyard that did make an eruv?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 6's ruling with a comparison
steps.raayaObject: That both courtyards are forbidden to use the חורבה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The accepted rule that a courtyard without an עירוב is not given to a courtyard with an עירוב

steps.title: Rejection: house utensils are kept in a courtyard but not in a ruin
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. In a courtyard, house utensils are normally kept, so people might bring them out and carry them over. In a ruin, utensils are not kept, so nobody will bring them there.
steps.simpleTranslation: There (two courtyards), since house utensils are kept safely in a courtyard, people may come to bring them out. Here, with a ruin, since utensils are not kept safely in a ruin, people will not come to bring them out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from step 7 by showing the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason a courtyard without an עירוב is not given to one with an עירוב is a specific worry. House utensils are kept in courtyards, so they might get carried out and into the other courtyard. A ruin is not a safe place to leave things, so that worry does not exist there. The proof falls apart, though it does not prove the opposite view.

keyTerms.meaning: They will come to take [them] out
A ruin (an abandoned, broken-down building or lot)

steps.confusionAlert: This rejection only knocks down the proof. It does not decide that both courtyards are permitted. That view comes only in the second version (איכא דאמרי).

phrases.english: There, since [they] are kept safe,
house utensils in a courtyard,
they will come to take [them] out.
Here, with a ruin,
since [they] are not kept safe,
courtyard utensils in a ruin,
they will not come to take [them] out.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּמִנַּטְרִי מָאנֵי דְבָתִּים בְּחָצֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 7
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from neighboring courtyards; the ruling itself is not disproven
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The worry about house utensils applies to a courtyard, where things are kept, but not to a ruin, where things are not kept

steps.title: Second version: חייא בר רב says both courtyards are permitted
steps.stepSummary: Some report חייא בר רב's view differently. The ruin belongs also to the courtyard with an עירוב, and both courtyards may use it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: חייא בר רב said the ruin belongs even to the courtyard that made an עירוב, and both are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version (איכא דאמרי) of חייא בר רב's opinion, which reaches the opposite result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, both courtyards share the ruin, just like before. But instead of forbidding each other, both may use it. This version builds on the same reasoning the גמרא used in step 8: a ruin carries no worry of bringing out house utensils.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say (introduces a different version of a teaching)

phrases.aramaic: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, חִיָּיא בַּר רַב אָמַר:
phrases.english: Some say: Chiyya bar Rav said:
[The ruin is given] even to the one that made an eruv,
and both are permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, חִיָּיא בַּר רַב אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different version of the opinion in step 6, reaching the opposite result
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both courtyards share the חורבה and both may use it.

steps.title: Possible challenge: a courtyard without an עירוב is not given to a courtyard with one
steps.stepSummary: Inside the second version, a challenge is raised. Maybe both should be forbidden, since a courtyard without an עירוב is not given to a courtyard with one.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say both should be forbidden, because we do not give a courtyard that did not make an עירוב to a courtyard that did make one...
steps.whatsHappening: The second version raises a possible objection to its own lenient ruling and sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same comparison used as a proof in step 7, but now it serves as a challenge to the lenient view. If a courtyard with an עירוב cannot use a neighboring courtyard without one, perhaps it also cannot use the ruin.

keyTerms.meaning: Because we do not give / assign

phrases.english: And if you say: both are forbidden —
because we do not give
a courtyard that did not make an eruv to a courtyard that did make an eruv.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a challenge against the lenient ruling of step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in step 9 that both courtyards may use the חורבה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A courtyard with an עירוב cannot use a courtyard without one, so it should not be able to use the ruin either

steps.title: Answer: the Sages forbade courtyards only because house utensils are kept there
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the Sages did not allow a neighboring courtyard because house utensils are kept in courtyards and might be carried out. Utensils are not kept in a ruin, so there is no such worry.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, since house utensils are kept safely in a courtyard, the Sages did not permit it, because people might come to take them out. But in a ruin, things are not kept safely.
steps.whatsHappening: The second version answers the challenge, using the same difference between a courtyard and a ruin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule about neighboring courtyards is based on one worry: house utensils kept in the courtyard. A ruin is not a place where people keep things, so the reason for being strict is missing. That is why both courtyards may use the ruin.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages did not permit them
But (marks the contrast between the two cases)

steps.whatToRemember: Both versions of חייא בר רב agree that the ruin belongs to both courtyards. They argue only whether both are forbidden or both are permitted. Either way, the key difference is that utensils are kept in a courtyard but not in a ruin.

phrases.english: There, since [they] are kept safe,
house utensils in a courtyard —
the Sages did not permit them,
since they might come to take [them] out.
But in a ruin, [utensils] are not kept safe.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּמִנַּטְרִי מָאנֵי דְבָתִּים בְּחָצֵר — לָא שָׁרוּ בְּהוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A ruin should be treated like a neighboring courtyard, so both are forbidden
steps.terutzMaskana: The courtyard rule rests on the worry about house utensils kept there. That worry does not apply to a ruin, so both courtyards are permitted.

steps.title: New משנה: a large roof or courtyard next to a small one
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: when a large roof is next to a small roof, or a large courtyard is breached into a small one, the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden. The reason is that the opening counts as the large one's doorway.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A large roof next to a small one: the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden. A large courtyard that was breached into a small one: the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden, because the breach is like the doorway of the large one.
steps.whatsHappening: The discussion of the ruin is finished, and a new משנה begins with a new case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening only partly breaks the large courtyard's wall, since wall remains on both sides of it. So it looks like a normal doorway, and the large courtyard keeps its walls. For the small courtyard, the opening takes up its whole side. That side has no wall left, so the small one is open to the large one and becomes forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: That was breached (part of its wall broke open)

steps.confusionAlert: It is the same opening for both courtyards, yet it affects them differently. For the large one it is only a gap in the middle of a wall (a doorway). For the small one it is the entire wall that is missing.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
A large roof next to a small one —
the large one is permitted, and the small one is forbidden.
A large courtyard that was breached into a small one —
the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden,
because it (the breach) is like the doorway of the large one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה after the ruin discussion is complete
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a large area opens into a small one, the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden, because the opening counts as the large one's doorway.

steps.title: Why does the משנה teach the same rule twice?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה needed both the roof case and the courtyard case, since they seem to teach the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why does it need to teach two cases?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה from Step 12 by asking why it lists two cases that seem identical. This question sets up the next two steps, where רב and שמואל each answer it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a large roof next to a small roof, and a large courtyard breached into a small one, both follow the same rule. If the rule is the same, one case should have been enough. The גמרא assumes the משנה never repeats itself for nothing, so the second case must teach something extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גְּמָרָא: the discussion of the משנה begins here
Why does it need this? (a question about something that seems unnecessary)

phrases.english: GEMARA:
phrases.notes: Marks the start of the גמרא's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: Why does it need to teach two cases?
phrases.notes: The two cases are roofs and courtyards

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's analysis of the משנה quoted in Step 12
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra lesson does the משנה teach by listing both the roof case and the courtyard case?

steps.title: According to רב, a roof's walls must be visible like a courtyard's
steps.stepSummary: רב reads the repetition as comparing a roof to a courtyard: just as a courtyard's walls are visible, the roof's walls must be visible too.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רב, the משנה teaches that a roof is like a courtyard. Just as a courtyard's walls are visible, so too a roof's walls must be visible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question according to רב. The משנה put the two cases side by side to teach that a roof follows the rule of a courtyard in one specific way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב allows carrying on a roof by imagining the walls of the house rising up to enclose it (גוד אסיק מחיצתא). The comparison to a courtyard adds a condition: this works only when the walls are visible, meaning the roof does not stick out past the walls of the house. So the second case is not extra; it sets this condition.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the same משנה can be read in line with each אמורא's earlier view on roofs.

phrases.english: According to Rav, it teaches a roof similar to a courtyard:
Just as a courtyard, its partition is visible,
so too a roof, its partition must also be visible.
phrases.notes: The roof must not extend beyond the house walls

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 13 according to רב
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The roof case is compared to the courtyard case: a roof is permitted only when its walls are visible, just like a courtyard's.

steps.title: According to שמואל, the roof is one where many people walk, like a courtyard
steps.stepSummary: שמואל reads the same comparison differently: just as many people walk through a courtyard, the משנה's roof is one where many people walk.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to שמואל, a roof is like a courtyard. Just as many people walk through a courtyard, so too the roof here is one that many people walk on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer to the same question, this time according to שמואל. He also compares the roof to the courtyard, but on a different point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, the משנה forbids the small roof only when it is used by many people, the way a courtyard is. If few people use the roof, even the small one would be permitted. So the courtyard comparison limits when the strict ruling applies.
steps.confusionAlert: Both רב and שמואל use the same words, 'a roof is like a courtyard,' but they compare different features. For רב it is about visible walls. For שמואל it is about how many people walk there.

phrases.english: And according to Shmuel, a roof is similar to a courtyard:

phrases.aramaic: מָה חָצֵר דְּקָא דָרְסִי לַהּ רַבִּים,
phrases.english: just as a courtyard is one that many people tread upon,

phrases.aramaic: אַף גַּג נָמֵי דְּקָא דָרְסִי לֵיהּ רַבִּים.
phrases.english: so too the roof is one that many people tread upon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives שמואל's answer to Step 13, alongside רב's answer in Step 14
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The roof case is compared to the courtyard case: the strict ruling applies to a roof that many people walk on, like a courtyard.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה repeats itself to compare a roof to a courtyard. רב says the comparison is about visible walls, and שמואל says it is about heavy use by many people.

steps.title: The sages infer that residents of the large courtyard count in the small one, but not the reverse
steps.stepSummary: רבה, רבי זירא and רבה בר רב חנן, with אביי sitting near them, learn from the משנה that residents of the large courtyard count as living in the small one, but residents of the small courtyard do not count in the large one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה, רבי זירא and רבה בר רב חנן were sitting, and אביי was sitting beside them. They said: Learn from the משנה that the residents of the large courtyard count in the small one, but the residents of the small courtyard do not count in the large one.
steps.whatsHappening: A group of sages draws a new rule out of the משנה. This sets up a discussion of what this inference means in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the large courtyard is permitted and the small one is forbidden. The sages explain why: the people of the large courtyard can walk freely into the small one, so they count as its residents and forbid it. The people of the small one do not count in the large one, so they do not forbid it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle explains the reason behind the משנה's ruling and becomes the basis for the next part of the discussion.

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַבָּה וְרַבִּי זֵירָא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב חָנָן,
phrases.english: Rabba, Rabbi Zeira, and Rabba bar Rav Ḥanan were sitting,
and Abaye was sitting beside them,
and they sat and said:
Learn from our mishna
that residents of the large one count in the small one,
but residents of the small one do not count in the large one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the רב and שמואל discussion and draws a new principle from the משנה of Step 12
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Residents of the large courtyard are considered residents of the small one, but residents of the small courtyard are not considered residents of the large one.

steps.title: Example: vines in the large courtyard forbid sowing in the small one
steps.stepSummary: The teaching illustrates its one-way rule with כלאי הכרם. Vines in the large courtyard make it forbidden to sow seeds in the small courtyard. If someone sowed there anyway, the seeds are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does this work? If there are vines in the large courtyard, it is forbidden to plant seeds in the small courtyard. And if he did plant, the seeds are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a practical example of the rule from Step 16. It uses the laws of planting seeds near a vineyard (כלאי הכרם).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 16 said the large courtyard 'counts' inside the small one. So vines in the large courtyard are treated as if they reach into the small courtyard, even when the seeds are planted some distance away. That puts seeds in the small courtyard in a forbidden mix with the vines, and the seeds become אסור.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? This word introduces an example that explains a general rule.
The seeds are forbidden. Once mixed with a vineyard, they may not be used.
The prohibition against planting grain or vegetables together with grapevines

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the vines are physically growing inside the small courtyard. They are only in the large one. The small courtyard is treated as if it belongs to the large one, so the vines 'reach' it legally.
steps.whyThisMatters: This example shows that the one-way rule about the two courtyards applies beyond עירובין, including to כלאים. It makes the abstract idea that the large one counts in the small one concrete and practical.

phrases.english: How so? If there are vines in the large courtyard —
phrases.notes: 'How so' signals that an example of Step 16's rule is coming.

phrases.english: it is forbidden to sow seeds in the small courtyard.
phrases.notes: This is because the small courtyard is treated as part of the large one, where the vines are.

phrases.english: and if he sowed, the seeds are forbidden,
phrases.notes: After the fact, the seeds become forbidden as כלאי הכרם. The teaching continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step illustrates Step 16's principle, that the large courtyard counts in the small one but not the reverse, with a practical case from כלאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vines in the large courtyard make it forbidden to sow in the small courtyard. If someone sowed there, the seeds are forbidden.
